back: It allows countries to **sell their resources and invest the money** in things such as education and healthcare, and to import resources they lack.

front:
**True or False?**

Trade agreements usually favour developing countries.
back:
**False.**

Trade agreements often favour **developed and emerging countries**, and developing countries are often paid less for their exports.

front: Define **tied aid**.
back: Aid that means countries **have to spend the money in specific ways** rather than on the development that is actually needed.

front: For aid to be **______**, it must fit the needs of the developing country.
back: For aid to be **appropriate**, it must fit the needs of the developing country.

front: Why does international aid not always reach the people who need it?
back: Because of **corruption and mismanagement**.

front: Name two forms in which international aid can be given.
back: Any two of: **advice, technology, food, money**.

front: How can a donor country misuse aid?
back: It can be used to apply **political or economic pressure** on the receiving country.

front: What does the World Trade Organisation (WTO) aim to do for its members?
back: Help members use trade to **raise living standards, create jobs** and improve people's lives.

front:
**True or False?**

Developing countries dominate the WTO.
back:
**False.**

**Developed countries and the largest economies** dominate the WTO.

front: The main exports from developing countries are usually **______**, which do not create the same profits as manufactured products.
back: The main exports from developing countries are usually **primary goods**, which do not create the same profits as manufactured products.

front: Define **debt relief**.
back: **Reducing or writing off the payments** a country has to make to donor countries, freeing up money for development.

front: What did the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative aim to ensure?
back: That **no country faces a debt burden it cannot manage**.

front: The Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative allowed for **______** debt relief on money owed to the IMF, World Bank or African Development Fund.
back: The Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative allowed for **100%** debt relief on money owed to the IMF, World Bank or African Development Fund.

front: How can debt relief help a country develop?
back: The money saved can be spent on **development, such as infrastructure, education and healthcare**.

front: In how many countries does the Fair Trade system work with farmers?
back: **73 countries**, working with over 1.9 million farmers.

front: In 2020, **______** was paid in Fair Trade premiums.
back: In 2020, **£169 million** was paid in Fair Trade premiums.

front: Define **microcredit**.
back: **Loans given to people to start a small business**, usually to people on very low incomes who would not get a bank loan.

front: What size are microcredit loans typically to start with?
back: Usually small, around **US\$100–500**, increasing as the business grows.

front: What are interest rates like on microcredit loans?
back: **Very low, or in some cases interest-free**.

front: Define a **top-down development** scheme.
back: A usually **expensive scheme run by governments or TNCs**, often funded by borrowing, in which local people have little say.

front: Define a **bottom-up development** scheme.
back: A relatively **low-cost scheme organised by NGOs and/or local people**, targeting the poorest communities using appropriate technology.

front: What is the main aim of HS2 in the UK?
back: To **reduce regional inequality** by increasing growth, productivity and incomes in the Midlands and the North of England.

front: The first stage of HS2 will link Birmingham and **______**.
back: The first stage of HS2 will link Birmingham and **London**.

front: Give one argument in favour of HS2.
back: It will **increase employment and productivity** in the Midlands and North, creating over 22,000 construction jobs.

front: Give one environmental argument against HS2.
back: Over **250 acres of green belt land** will be built on, and it will cross Sites of Special Scientific Interest.

front:
**True or False?**

Local people affected by top-down schemes usually have a large say in the process.
back:
**False.**

Local people affected by top-down schemes often have **little say** in the process.

front: What is the aim of the micro-hydro schemes in Peru?
back: To **provide electricity to remote rural areas**, where 50% of people were living on just US\$2 a day.

front: Practical Action has installed **______** micro-hydro schemes across Peru.
back: Practical Action has installed **47** micro-hydro schemes across Peru.

front: How many families receive metered electricity from the Peru micro-hydro schemes?
back: **5,000 families**.

front: Which organisations helped pay for the Chambamontera micro-hydro scheme?
back: The **community, Japan and Practical Action**, at a cost of US\$51,000.

front: Give one benefit that electricity brought to Chambamontera.
back: Any one of: **streetlights allowing people out after dark, improved school facilities, homework in the evening, business development, mechanised coffee processing**.

front: Define **quantitative data** in a river study.
back: **Numerical data** collected in a river enquiry, such as **channel measurements**, **sediment size**, **width**, **depth**, **velocity**, and calculated **discharge** values.

front: Define **qualitative data** in river fieldwork.
back: Non-numerical, **descriptive data** such as **field sketches**, **photographs**, and written observations of **river features** and **landforms**.

front: Where should river **width** be measured?
back: Measure **width** from where the **dry bank meets the water** on one side directly across to where the **dry bank meets the water** on the opposite side.

front: When measuring width, the tape must be held <u>         </u> and not touch the <u>       </u>.
back: When measuring width, the tape must be held **taut** and not touch the **water**.

front: Why is river **depth** measured at regular intervals across the channel?
back: Regular intervals give a **full picture** of depth changes and allow calculation of a reliable **mean depth** for **discharge** calculations.

front: How is **velocity** measured using a **float**?
back: Time a **float** over a known distance (e.g. 10 m) using a **stopwatch**, repeat three times at each position, then calculate **mean velocity**.

front: What is the formula for **river discharge**?
back:
$Q = A \times v$

- $Q$ = discharge (m^3/s)
- $A$ = cross-sectional area (m^2)
- $v$ = mean velocity (m/s)

front: To calculate cross-sectional area, multiply river <u>     </u> by mean <u>         </u>.
back: To calculate cross-sectional area, multiply river **width** by mean **depth**.

front:
**True or False?**

Field sketches and photographs are **quantitative** river data.
back:
**False.**

Field sketches and photographs are **qualitative** data because they provide **descriptive visual information**, not numerical measurements.

front: Define **aim** in a river enquiry.
back: A broad **statement of what the investigation intends to find out**, such as how **discharge** or **cross-profile** changes downstream.

front: Define **hypothesis** in river fieldwork.
back: A **testable statement or prediction** based on **geographical theory**, for example that **discharge increases** with distance downstream.

front: What is the **Bradshaw model** used for in river studies?
back: The **Bradshaw model** predicts how river characteristics like **width**, **depth**, **velocity**, and **discharge** change **from source to mouth**.

front: In **systematic sampling**, sites are chosen at <u>           </u> intervals along the river.
back: In **systematic sampling**, sites are chosen at **regular** intervals along the river.

front:
**True or False?**

Random sampling helps reduce bias in river site selection.
back:
**True.**

**Random sampling** gives every potential site an **equal chance** of selection, which **reduces bias** in where data are collected.

front: State two risks of carrying out river fieldwork.
back: Two risks are **slippery rocks** and **flash flooding**.

front: Define **primary data**.
back: Data that is **collected by the student** completing the fieldwork.

front: Define **secondary data**.
back: All information that is **not collected by the student** completing the study.

front: Which type of graph is best for showing a **river channel cross-section**?
back: A **line graph**.

front: Which type of graph is used to **compare different sites**?
back: A **bar graph**.

front: Which graph shows the **relationship between two sets of data**, such as river width and discharge?
back: A **scattergraph**.

front: River discharge data used as secondary data can be obtained from the **______**.
back: River discharge data used as secondary data can be obtained from the **Environment Agency**.

front: Weather data for a river enquiry can be obtained from the **______**.
back: Weather data for a river enquiry can be obtained from the **Meteorological Office (Met Office)**.

front: Why are **Ordnance Survey maps** useful as secondary data in a river enquiry?
back: They enable the **identification of sample site locations**.

front:
**True or False?**

River width, depth and velocity data is qualitative.
back:
**False.**

Width, depth and velocity data is **quantitative** and is analysed using statistical methods.

front: Which statistical method is mainly used to analyse river depth or velocity data?
back: The **mean**.

front: How is the **mean** of a data set calculated?
back: **Add all the values together**, then **divide by the number of values** in the data set.

front: Are photographs and field sketches a quantitative or qualitative analysis method?
back: **Qualitative** analysis.

front: What should a fieldwork conclusion state about the hypothesis?
back: Whether the hypothesis has been **proved or disproved**.

front: Define **anomaly** in fieldwork data.
back: A result that **does not fit the pattern** of the other measurements, which may occur naturally or result from **incorrect recording or human error**.

front: The final stage of the river enquiry is the **______**, where you note how successful the investigation was.
back: The final stage of the river enquiry is the **evaluation**, where you note how successful the investigation was.

front: Define **hypothesis**.
back: A **statement** that is tested through fieldwork.

front: Define **null hypothesis**.
back: A statement that is the **opposite of a hypothesis**, used to ensure there is **no bias** when collecting evidence.

front: Why must an aim be **focused** on a particular place?
back: Because you **cannot measure everywhere**.

front: State two risks specific to **coastal fieldwork**.
back: Any two of: **tide times**, **weather conditions**, **slippery rocks**, **polluted water**, working in an unfamiliar place or misuse of equipment.

front: How could the risk of **infection from dirty water** be managed?
back: **Wash hands**, use antibacterial hand wash and **cover cuts and wounds**.

front: In **systematic sampling**, how are sites selected?
back: At **regular intervals**, so that all parts of the stretch of coast are covered.

front: Why does **random sampling** reduce bias?
back: All sites have an **equal chance** of being selected.

front: **______** sampling divides each sampling site into groups, such as three sites from each sample section.
back: **Stratified** sampling divides each sampling site into groups, such as three sites from each sample section.

front: Which piece of equipment is used to measure a **beach gradient**?
back: A **clinometer**.

front: What is a **quadrat** used for in coastal fieldwork?
back: To **select sediment for sampling**.

front: Define **beach profile**.
back: A survey using **distance and angle measurements** to identify the **shape of the beach**.

front: Which equipment is used to measure the axes of a pebble in **sediment analysis**?
back: **Callipers**.

front: Which coastal process is examined through **sediment analysis** across a beach?
back: **Longshore drift**.

front: When measuring longshore drift, pebbles are marked with waterproof paint and placed in the **______** zone.
back: When measuring longshore drift, pebbles are marked with waterproof paint and placed in the **swash** zone.

front:
**True or False?**

Photographs and field sketches are quantitative data.
back:
**False.**

Photographs and field sketches are **qualitative** data.

front: Which type of graph shows **continuous changes in data over time**?
back: A **line graph**.

front: Which graph shows a positive or negative **relationship between two variables**, such as sediment size and beach gradient?
back: A **scatter graph**.

front: A **______** graph shows data using rectangles drawn to a certain height, for example sediment size along a transect.
back: A **bar** graph shows data using rectangles drawn to a certain height, for example sediment size along a transect.

front: What weather secondary data is available from the **Met Office** for a coastal enquiry?
back: **Rainfall data**, giving information on weather events impacting the data collected.

front: What secondary data can a **geology map** provide for a coastal enquiry?
back: **Rock type information** for the coastal cliffs.

front: Define **Shoreline Management Plan (SMP)**.
back: A source of **secondary data** from local authorities, the Environment Agency or the government used in a coastal enquiry.

front: Is beach slope and pebble size data quantitative or qualitative?
back: **Quantitative**, so it is analysed using statistical methods.

front: Define the **median** of a data set.
back: The **middle value** in a set of data, found by organising the data in order from **smallest to largest**.

front: How do you calculate the **mean** beach gradient?
back: **Add all the values together**, then **divide by the total number** of data sets.

front:
**True or False?**

Analysing photographs and field sketches is quantitative analysis.
back:
**False.**

Analysing photographs and field sketches is **qualitative** analysis.

front: What should a coastal enquiry **conclusion** state about the hypothesis?
back: Whether the hypothesis has been **proved or disproved**.

front: A pebble sample taken near a **______** may be an anomaly because it is protected from wave action.
back: A pebble sample taken near a **groyne** may be an anomaly because it is protected from wave action.

front: What does the **evaluation** stage of a coastal enquiry consider?
back: How **successful** the investigation was and what you would do **differently** next time.

front: Hazardous environment fieldwork is based on the physical processes of what?
back: An **extreme weather event**.

front: Name two geographical theories a weather fieldwork enquiry can be linked to.
back: **Microclimate** and the **passage of a depression** or tropical storm.

front: Define **systematic sampling** in a weather enquiry.
back: Sampling of sites at **regular intervals** along a transect line.

front: In **______** sampling, all sites have an equal chance of being selected, for example using a grid placed across a map of the school site.
back: In **random** sampling, all sites have an equal chance of being selected, for example using a grid placed across a map of the school site.

front: Which instrument measures **wind speed**?
back: An **anemometer**.

front: Which instrument measures **air pressure**?
back: A **barometer**.

front: Which instrument measures **humidity**?
back: A **hygrometer**.

front: State two risks associated specifically with **weather fieldwork**.
back: Any two of: **weather conditions**, slipping on uneven ground, working in an unfamiliar place, **misuse of equipment** (mercury thermometers) or traffic.

front: Define **Stevenson screen**.
back: A **housing** for weather instruments that allows air temperature in the **shade** to be recorded, protecting instruments and ensuring accuracy.

front: Which three instruments should be placed in a **Stevenson screen** to ensure accuracy?
back: The **thermometer, hygrometer and barometer**.

front: Define **weather diary**.
back: A **record of weather conditions** over a set period.

front: Which thermometer gives the maximum and minimum readings over 24 hours?
back: A **maximum and minimum thermometer**.

front: A **______** is used to give the direction the wind is coming from.
back: A **wind vane** is used to give the direction the wind is coming from.

front: In what units does an **anemometer** measure wind speed?

**True or False?**

A rain gauge measures the amount of rainfall in centimetres.
back:
**False.**

A rain gauge measures the amount of rainfall in **millimetres (mm)**.

front: Which graph type is most suitable for showing changes in **temperature** over time in a weather enquiry?
back: A **line graph**.

front: Which type of graph is used to show **wind direction and speed** in a weather enquiry?
back: A **rose graph**.

front: What is a **scattergraph** used to show in a weather enquiry?
back: The **relationship** between two factors, such as **air pressure and precipitation**.

front: In a weather enquiry, **______** graphs are suitable for presenting precipitation and wind speed data.
back: In a weather enquiry, **bar** graphs are suitable for presenting precipitation and wind speed data.

front: Which type of map is used to show temperature and precipitation in a weather enquiry?
back: An **isoline map**.

front: Define **secondary data**.
back: Data collected by **someone else**, such as **Met Office** records, newspaper articles, Ordnance Survey maps or aerial photographs.

front: Name one organisation that provides secondary weather data for a weather enquiry.
back: The **Meteorological Office (Met Office)**.

front:
**True or False?**

An Ordnance Survey map can be used to identify the altitude of a sample site.
back:
**True.**

An OS map gives the **altitude** of a site, and compass directions give its **aspect**.

front: Which statistical method is used to calculate average wind speed, temperature or rainfall in a weather enquiry?
back: The **mean**.

front: Weather data such as temperature and precipitation is **______** data, analysed using statistical methods.
back: Weather data such as temperature and precipitation is **quantitative** data, analysed using statistical methods.

front:
**True or False?**

Using photographs and field sketches is a form of quantitative analysis.
back:
**False.**

Using photographs and field sketches is a form of **qualitative** analysis.

front: In the conclusion of a weather enquiry, what should be stated about the hypothesis?
back: Whether the hypothesis has been **proven or disproved**.

front: Define **anomaly**.
back: A result that **does not fit the pattern** of the other data, caused by a natural cause or by **human error** in recording.

front: What is the final step of a weather enquiry after reaching a conclusion?
back: The **evaluation**, where you assess the investigation's success and what you would change if repeating it.

front: What is the focus of the economic activity and energy fieldwork enquiry?
back: **Developing energy resources**.

front: Why is **sampling** used when selecting sites for an energy enquiry?
back: To **reduce bias**, as it is not practical to study every area or ask every person.

front: Define **stratified sampling** for a questionnaire.
back: Sampling where the population selected is **representative of the whole** population, e.g. if 10% are over 65, then 10% of the sample is over 65.

front: In **______** sampling, data is collected at regular intervals around the energy development.
back: In **systematic** sampling, data is collected at regular intervals around the energy development.

front: How can a site location be recorded to give an accurate position?
back: Using **GPS** to give latitude and longitude.

front: State two health and safety risks of an energy fieldwork enquiry.
back: Any two of: **traffic accidents**, mugging/crime, an **unfamiliar environment**, getting lost or construction sites.

front: What is the only measuring instrument used in the field for an energy enquiry?
back: A **digital decibel meter**.

front: What are **questionnaires** used to gather in an energy enquiry?
back: The **attitudes and opinions** of local people, for example towards a wind farm expansion.

front: Define a **closed question**.
back: A question with a **limited, fixed set of answers**, e.g. 'How long have you lived in this area?'

front: Define an **open question**.
back: A question that allows a **free, detailed response**, e.g. 'What are your views on the expansion of the wind farm?'

front: What is an **environmental quality survey (EQS)** used for?
back: To **compare different sites** around the energy development.

front: Why is a **questionnaire** a useful data collection method?
back: It can provide a **mix of qualitative and quantitative data** through open and closed questions.

front:
**True or False?**

Photographs and field sketches are quantitative data.
back:
**False.**

Photographs and field sketches are **qualitative data**.

front: When completing an environmental quality survey, care must be taken to be as **______** as possible.
back: When completing an environmental quality survey, care must be taken to be as **objective** as possible.

front: Which graph is used to **compare environmental quality scores** at different sites?
back: A **bar graph**.

front: Which graph shows the relationship between **distance from the energy development** and environmental quality?
back: A **scattergraph**.

front: Which type of chart is used to show people's **views and opinions** on an energy development?
back: A **pie chart**.

front: On a pie chart, every 1% is equal to **______** degrees.
back: On a pie chart, every 1% is equal to **3.6** degrees.

front: What can a map with **proportional circles** show in an energy enquiry?
back: Different **opinions** towards the energy development at different sites.

front: State two sources of **secondary data** for an energy enquiry.
back: Any two of: **maps** of the area, **newspaper/website articles** about energy development, or aerial photographs.

front: Is questionnaire and environmental quality survey data quantitative or qualitative?
back: **Quantitative**, so it is analysed using statistical methods.

front: Define the **mode** of a data set.
back: The **most common result** in a set of data.

front: What does a **best-fit line** identify?
back: The **trend** in the relationship between two variables.

front: Define a **negative correlation**.
back: A relationship where, **as one factor increases, the other falls**.

front:
**True or False?**

Analysing photographs and field sketches is a quantitative technique.
back:
**False.**

Using photographs and field sketches is a **qualitative** analysis.

front: What should the **conclusion** of an energy enquiry state?
back: Whether the hypothesis has been **proven or disproved**.

front: To make sure all questions are clear, a questionnaire can be tested using a **______** study.
back: To make sure all questions are clear, a questionnaire can be tested using a **pilot** study.

front: What may cause an **anomaly** in energy fieldwork results?
back: A **natural cause**, or **incorrect recording or human error**.

front: Which geographical theory can the rural fieldwork enquiry be linked to?
back: **Counter-urbanisation** and rural environmental change.

front: Give two reasons why **sampling** is used in a rural enquiry.
back: It **reduces bias** and provides an **overview of the whole**.

front: Define **opportunistic sampling**.
back: Sampling used when access is **limited**, taking data from the **nearest accessible site** to the one selected.

front: In **______** sampling, a grid is placed across the rural area so all sites have an equal chance of being selected.
back: In **random** sampling, a grid is placed across the rural area so all sites have an equal chance of being selected.

front: How can a site location be recorded accurately in a rural enquiry?
back: Using **GPS** to give latitude and longitude.

front: State two risks associated specifically with **rural environment fieldwork**.
back: Any two of: **weather conditions**, uneven ground, working in an unfamiliar place, traffic or **livestock**.

front: How could the risk from **livestock** in fields be managed?
back: Only entering fields where there is **no livestock**.

front: What is the only measuring instrument used in the field for a rural enquiry?
back: A **digital decibel meter**.

front: What is a **traffic and pedestrian flow survey** used for?
back: To **compare traffic and pedestrian levels** at different sample sites and times of day.

front: A traffic or pedestrian flow survey can be recorded on a **______** chart.
back: A traffic or pedestrian flow survey can be recorded on a **tally** chart.

front: What is an **environmental quality survey (EQS)** used to do in a rural enquiry?
back: To **compare different sites** within the rural area.

front: Define a **statement question** in a questionnaire.
back: A question giving a statement to which the respondent replies **strongly agree, agree, disagree or strongly disagree**.

front:
**True or False?**

Photographs and field sketches are quantitative data.
back:
**False.**

Photographs and field sketches are **qualitative data**.

front: Why are **field sketches** a useful form of primary data?
back: They **capture lots of detail** that can be examined after the trip and are **easy to annotate** to help with analysis.

front: Which graph is used to compare **environmental quality scores** at different sample sites?
back: A **bar graph**.

front: Which type of bar graph is used to show **traffic counts**?
back: A **compound or divided bar graph**.

front: Which diagram is used to show **noise levels** in a rural enquiry?
back: A **rose diagram**.

front: A **______** circle map can be used to show traffic counts at different sample sites.
back: A **proportional** circle map can be used to show traffic counts at different sample sites.

front: Which graph shows the relationship between **proximity to land use change** and environmental quality?
back: A **scattergraph**.

front: State two sources of **secondary data** for a rural environment enquiry.
back: Any two of: **historical traffic counts**, **maps** of the area, newspaper/website articles, aerial photographs or census data.

front: How can **census data** help when planning a rural questionnaire?
back: It gives the **population structure**, so a **fair sampling frame** can be designed.

front: Are environmental quality survey and traffic count data quantitative or qualitative?
back: **Quantitative**, so they are analysed using statistical methods.

front: Define the **range** of a data set.
back: The **difference between the highest and lowest values** in the data set.

front: How do you calculate the **range** of environmental quality scores?
back: Subtract the **lowest score from the highest score**.

front:
**True or False?**

Using photographs and field sketches is a quantitative analysis method.
back:
**False.**

Using photographs and field sketches is **qualitative analysis**.

front: Give an example of an **anomaly** in rural fieldwork data.
back: A sample site with a **low traffic count but high levels of noise pollution**.

front: Completing an environmental quality survey alone is **______**; doing it in groups and taking the mode reduces this.
back: Completing an environmental quality survey alone is **subjective**; doing it in groups and taking the mode reduces this.

front: What should the **conclusion** of a rural enquiry state?
back: Whether the hypothesis has been **proven or disproved**.

front: Which two theories can the urban fieldwork enquiry be linked to?
back: Changes in **urban land use** and **sustainability**.

front: Give an example of a **hypothesis** for an urban enquiry.
back: **Environmental quality improves with distance from the CBD**.

front: Define **null hypothesis**.
back: A statement that is the **opposite of a hypothesis**, used to ensure there is **no bias** when collecting evidence.

front: Give two reasons why **sampling** is used in an urban enquiry.
back: It **reduces bias** and provides an **overview of the whole**.

front: Define **systematic sampling**.
back: Sampling of sites or people at **regular intervals** along a transect line.

front: In **______** sampling, if 10% of the population is over 65, then 10% of the sample should be over 65.
back: In **stratified** sampling, if 10% of the population is over 65, then 10% of the sample should be over 65.

front: State two risks associated specifically with **urban environment fieldwork**.
back: Any two of: **traffic/cars**, working in an unfamiliar place, getting lost, speaking to strangers or **pollution**.

front: How could working in **groups** help manage risk during urban fieldwork?
back: It ensures **safety against unexpected events**.

front: What is the only measuring instrument used in the field for an urban enquiry?
back: A **digital decibel meter**.

front: State two types of **quantitative data** used in an urban land use change enquiry.
back: Any two of: **environmental surveys**, **traffic/pedestrian surveys** or **closed questions** from questionnaires.

front: What is an **environmental quality survey (EQS)** used to do in an urban enquiry?
back: To **compare different sites** within the urban area.

front: A traffic and pedestrian flow survey is recorded on a **______** chart at different sites and times of the day.
back: A traffic and pedestrian flow survey is recorded on a **tally** chart at different sites and times of the day.

front:
**True or False?**

Photographs and field sketches are quantitative data.
back:
**False.**

Photographs and field sketches are **qualitative data**.

front: Define an **open question**.
back: A question allowing a **free, detailed response**, e.g. 'What are your views on the new housing development?'

front: Which graph compares **environmental quality scores** at different urban sample sites?
back: A **bar graph**.

front: Which type of bar graph is used to present **traffic counts**?
back: A **compound or divided bar graph**.

front: **______** diagrams are used to show noise levels in an urban enquiry.
back: **Rose** diagrams are used to show noise levels in an urban enquiry.

front: What can a **proportional circle** map show in an urban enquiry?
back: **Traffic counts** at different sample sites.

front: State two sources of **secondary data** for an urban environment enquiry.
back: Any two of: **historical traffic counts**, **maps** of the area, newspaper/website articles or aerial photographs.

front: How does secondary data help with **spatial variation** in a study area?
back: It ensures **good spatial coverage** to minimise bias.

front: Are environmental quality survey and traffic count data quantitative or qualitative?
back: **Quantitative**, so they are analysed using statistical methods.

front: Define the **range** of a data set.
back: The **difference between the highest and lowest values** in the data set.

front: Which statistical method gives a measure of centrality by averaging the data?
back: The **mean**.

front: Why are **photographs** a useful source of primary data?
back: They **capture lots of detail** and give an **accurate representation** of the site at that point in time.

front:
**True or False?**

Using photographs and field sketches is a quantitative analysis method.
back:
**False.**

Using photographs and field sketches is a **qualitative** analysis.

front: What should the **conclusion** of an urban enquiry state?
back: Whether the hypothesis has been **proven or disproved**.

front: An anomaly might be a sample site with a low traffic count but high levels of **______** pollution.
back: An anomaly might be a sample site with a low traffic count but high levels of **noise** pollution.

front: What does the **evaluation** stage of an urban enquiry outline?
back: How **successful** the enquiry was and what could be done **differently** if repeated.

front: Define **aim** (in fieldwork).
back: A statement explaining **what the enquiry is attempting to achieve**.

front: Define **hypothesis**.
back: A **clear, directional and measurable** statement that can be **tested**.

front: What are the three qualities a good hypothesis must have?
back: It must be **clear, directional and measurable**.

front: How many stages are there in the enquiry process?
back: **Six** stages.

front: The six stages of the enquiry process are planning, methods and data collection, data presentation, **______**, conclusions and evaluation.
back: The six stages of the enquiry process are planning, methods and data collection, data presentation, **analysis**, conclusions and evaluation.

front: Which model of rivers might a fieldwork hypothesis be based on?
back: **Bradshaw's model**.

front: Name one factor that determines the location chosen for fieldwork.
back: The **topic** of the enquiry, **distance**, **accessibility** or **suitability**.

front: The greater the **______** to a fieldwork site, the less time will be available for collecting data.
back: The greater the **distance** to a fieldwork site, the less time will be available for collecting data.

front: Once the fieldwork location has been decided, what is used to identify the sample sites within it?
back: **Sampling**.

front: Define **risk assessment**.
back: A consideration of **health and safety** in which **hazards are identified**, along with who is at risk and the **precautions** to reduce the risk.

front: How can the risk of contracting Weil's disease during river fieldwork be managed?
back: **Wash hands** after being in the water, **cover open wounds** and use **anti-bacterial hand wash**.

front: How can the risk of slipping on rocks during river fieldwork be reduced?
back: Wear **sturdy, appropriate footwear** with **good grips** on the sole.

front:
**True or False?**

A safety helmet should be worn when working below a cliff face.
back:
**True.**

You should wear a safety helmet below a cliff face, not climb the cliff, and not work at cliff faces in very wet or windy weather.

front:
**True or False?**

An aim is a statement that can be tested, while a hypothesis explains what the enquiry is trying to achieve.
back:
**False.**

It is the other way round: the **aim** explains what the enquiry is trying to achieve, while the **hypothesis** is the testable statement.

front: Why is sampling used in fieldwork instead of measuring the whole area?
back: There is **not enough time, equipment or access** to measure the whole area being examined.

front: Sampling provides a **______** and statistically valid sample of the whole.
back: Sampling provides a **representative** and statistically valid sample of the whole.

front: Name the three main types of sampling.
back: **Random**, **systematic** and **stratified**.

front: Define **systematic sampling**.
back: Selecting samples at **regular intervals**, for example every 500 metres or every tenth person.

front: Define **stratified sampling**.
back: Sampling used when the study area includes significantly different parts (**subsets**), so the sample reflects their proportions in the whole population.

front: In random sampling, how are the sample points selected?
back: Numbered grid squares over the study area are entered into a **random number generator**.

front: Which sampling method can be used when a sample site cannot be accessed?
back: **Opportunistic sampling**, using a site as close as possible to the inaccessible one.

front: Why is random sampling described as the least biased method?
back: **All possible sample sites have an equal chance** of being selected.

front: A disadvantage of systematic sampling is that not all sites have an equal chance of being selected, which increases the **______**.
back: A disadvantage of systematic sampling is that not all sites have an equal chance of being selected, which increases the **bias**.

front: State one advantage of systematic sampling.
back: It is **easy and quick** and covers the **whole study area equally**.

front: What must be known and accurate for stratified sampling to work?
back: The **proportions of the subsets**.

front:
**True or False?**

Random sampling guarantees that the sample fully represents the whole population.
back:
**False.**

Representation may be **poor** if the random sites miss large areas, and some selected sites may be inaccessible or unsafe.

front:
**True or False?**

Stratified sampling can be used alongside systematic and random sampling.
back:
**True.**

An advantage of stratified sampling is that it can be combined with systematic and random sampling, allowing comparisons between subsets.

front: Define **analysis** (of fieldwork data).
back: The process which makes sense of data by identifying **patterns, trends, connections and meaning**.

front: Which type of data is analysed using numerical and statistical methods?
back: **Quantitative** data.

front: Define **mean**.
back: The value found by **adding all the values** in a data set and **dividing by the number of values**.

front: Define **median**.
back: The **middle value** of a data set once the numbers are arranged in **rank order**.

front: Define **mode**.
back: The value which occurs **most frequently** in a data set.

front: What do the mean, median and mode all measure?
back: **Central tendency**.

front: Define **range**.
back: A measure of **dispersion**; the distance between the **highest and lowest** value.

front: The **______** range is the part of the range that covers the middle 50% of the data.
back: The **interquartile** range is the part of the range that covers the middle 50% of the data.

front: Define **anomaly** (in data analysis).
back: A result which **does not fit the pattern or trend** and needs to be described and explained.

front: What kind of analysis is the annotation of photographs and field sketches?
back: A **qualitative** analysis.

front: What does annotation add to the features shown in a photograph or field sketch?
back: It gives them **meaning** as part of the analysis.

front: Range is a measure of **______** – the spread of data around the average.
back: Range is a measure of **dispersion** – the spread of data around the average.

front:
**True or False?**

The median is the value that occurs most often in a data set.
back:
**False.**

The **mode** occurs most often; the **median** is the middle value in rank order.

front: What is the key focus of the fieldwork evaluation questions in the exam?
back: The **evaluation of data collection**.

front: Name one common limitation of fieldwork data collection.
back: **Accessibility** of sample sites, **sample size**, **duration**, equipment issues or human error.

front: Define **human error** (in data collection).
back: **Mistakes in recording data** or reading the equipment.

front: One improvement to data collection is increasing the **______** so that results are more accurate.
back: One improvement to data collection is increasing the **sample size** so that results are more accurate.

front: Which piece of equipment would be more accurate than a float for measuring river velocity?
back: A **flow meter**.

front: Give one example of an unforeseen issue that could affect fieldwork results on the day.
back: **Road works** or changes in **river flow**.

front: When evaluating conclusions, what should the conclusions be checked against?
back: Whether they reflect the **aims and hypothesis** set out at the start of the enquiry.

front: Besides increasing sample size, name one other way data collection could be improved.
back: Taking **more measurements** or looking at a **wider range of secondary sources**.

front: Enquiry evaluation should evaluate how **______** the conclusions were.
back: Enquiry evaluation should evaluate how **reliable** the conclusions were.

front: When evaluating the enquiry design, what should be asked about the hypothesis itself?
back: Whether it was **appropriate** and could be **easily assessed**.

front:
**True or False?**

Evaluation should only identify problems and not suggest improvements.
back:
**False.**

Evaluation should identify limitations **and** suggest other useful data or improvements that could be made.

front:
**True or False?**

Suggesting how the scope of the study could be extended is part of enquiry evaluation.
back:
**True.**

Evaluation should suggest how the **scope of the study could be extended**.
